batches.reply: Ugh, three retries hitting the same wall is exhausting. The good news is that a timeout that's identical every time usually means a config problem, not a flaky one, so retrying won't fix it. But it should be findable. Here's what most often causes it, roughly in order. First, the app is listening on the wrong port or address. If it's bound to localhost instead of zero point zero point zero point zero, or to a different port than the health check expects, the check never connects. Second, the health check path is wrong or needs auth. Check that it returns a two hundred, not a redirect or a four-oh-one. Third, the app just starts too slowly. Migrations, warming a cache, or pulling a big model can take longer than the grace period. Try raising the initial delay or the timeout. Fourth, the app is crashing on boot. A missing environment variable or secret in the new environment does this a lot. The container restarts, and all the health check sees is a timeout. Fifth, networking. A security group, firewall, or network policy blocks the health checker from reaching the container. The quickest way to narrow it down is to pull the container or app logs from one of the failed attempts. Did it print "listening on" anything, or did it die first? I can't see your deploy from here, so send me those logs, your platform, whether that's Kubernetes, E C S, Fly, Render or something else, and your health check config. And tell me what changed since the last good deploy. We'll find it.

batches.reply: Three identical timeouts tell us something useful. This isn't flaky, it's deterministic, so another retry won't fix it. The question is whether the app is up and the check can't reach it, or whether the app never gets healthy at all. The fastest way to split that: get a shell in the running container or instance and curl the health endpoint from inside. If it answers there but the check still times out, it's almost always one of three things. The app is listening on 127.0.0.1 instead of 0.0.0.0. The port in the health check doesn't match the port the app actually uses. Or a security group or firewall is blocking the checker. If it doesn't answer even from inside, look at the startup logs. The usual suspects are a startup that takes longer than the check's grace period, often because of migrations or a cold cache. Or the health endpoint is waiting on a database or other dependency it can't reach. Or the path redirects or needs auth, so it never sends back a clean 200. Send me the startup logs from the last attempt, the health check config, and where this is deployed, like ECS, Kubernetes, or Fly, and I'll help you narrow it down.

If it's a plain loop over the items, it's usually safest to loop over the list itself and skip the index counting.

batches.reply: I don't have any context on this deploy and no access to your systems from here, so I can't look at it myself. A health check that times out the same way three times in a row usually isn't flaky, though. Something is failing every time, and these are the usual causes, most likely first. First, the app may be listening in the wrong place. It might be bound to localhost instead of all interfaces, or on a different port than the health check is hitting. That gives you a clean timeout every time. Second, the app may start too slowly. If it takes longer to boot than the health check's grace period allows, it gets killed before it's ready. Look for an initial delay or startup grace setting and try raising it a lot. Third, the health endpoint may hang because it waits on something it can't reach, like the database, a secret, or another service. A new environment variable, a network rule or a credential change would cause this. Fourth, the app may be crashing on startup. Check whether the container restarts or exits. If it does, the timeout is just a symptom. The fastest way to tell which one it is: pull the logs from the failed instance and see whether the app ever says it's listening. Then, if you can, get a shell next to it and call the health endpoint yourself. If you tell me the platform, the error message, the app's startup logs and what changed since the last good deploy, I can narrow it down.

First, the app may just be starting slower than the health check allows. If the first check runs before the app has finished booting, warming caches or running migrations, it times out every time. Missing environment variables or secrets in the new release often cause this. Fourth, look for a network rule or security group blocking the health checker's traffic. This is especially likely if something about the infrastructure changed recently. The fastest way to narrow it down is to get a shell on the failing instance or container and request the health endpoint locally. If it responds there, the problem is networking or the port. If it hangs there too, the problem is in the app or one of its dependencies. batches.reply: Three identical timeouts is frustrating. It also tells us something: this isn't flaky. Something fails the same way every time, so another retry won't fix it. Here's what I'd check, most likely cause first. One. Is the app listening on zero zero zero zero, or only on localhost? An app bound to 127.0.0.1 looks healthy from inside the container, but the health checker can't reach it. This is the classic cause. Two. Does the port match? Check that the health check hits the same port the app actually listens on. Watch for a PORT environment variable that the platform sets but your app ignores. Three. Is startup slower than the grace period? Migrations, cache warming or a cold dependency at boot can push readiness past the timeout. Look at the timestamp of the app's "listening" log line and compare it to when the check gives up. Four. Does the health endpoint itself work? If it redirects, needs auth, or calls the database and hangs, the check never gets a clean 200. Five. Is the app crashing silently? A missing secret or environment variable can kill it before it ever answers. The quickest way to narrow it down is the container logs from one failed attempt. If the app never says it's listening, it's a crash or a slow start. If it does say it's listening, it's the bind address, the port, or the endpoint. Send me those logs, and tell me which platform you're deploying to, and I'll help you find it.

I don't have any context on this deploy and no access to your systems from here, so I can't look at it myself. A health check that times out the same way three times in a row usually isn't flaky, though. Something is failing every time, and these are the usual causes, most likely first.

First, the app may be listening in the wrong place. It might be bound to localhost instead of all interfaces, or on a different port than the health check is hitting. That gives you a clean timeout every time.

Second, the app may start too slowly. If it takes longer to boot than the health check's grace period allows, it gets killed before it's ready. Look for an initial delay or startup grace setting and try raising it a lot.

Third, the health endpoint may hang because it waits on something it can't reach, like the database, a secret, or another service. A new environment variable, a network rule or a credential change would cause this.

Fourth, the app may be crashing on startup. Check whether the container restarts or exits. If it does, the timeout is just a symptom.

The fastest way to tell which one it is: pull the logs from the failed instance and see whether the app ever says it's listening. Then, if you can, get a shell next to it and call the health endpoint yourself.

If you tell me the platform, the error message, the app's startup logs and what changed since the last good deploy, I can narrow it down.

That's a rough spot. I don't have any context on your system yet, so here's what to do first, and what I need from you.

Right now, before touching anything else:

First, stop all automation. Pause the deploy pipeline, any auto-rollback, and any autoscaling that might be launching new instances. Retrying a failed rollback is how half-and-half turns into a mess.

Second, post one short message in the on-call channel. Something like: "Deploy and rollback both failed, mixed versions in prod, I'm incident lead, updates every fifteen minutes, please hold off on changes." That quiets the noise and stops other people from making changes at the same time.

Third, figure out what's actually broken for users. Are errors spiking, or is it mostly working? That tells you whether you need to rush or whether you have time to do this carefully.

Then, the key question is why the rollback failed. It's almost always one of three things:

One. A database migration ran forward, and the old code doesn't work with the new schema. If so, don't roll back. Roll forward to the new version, or patch the old one so it works with the new schema.

Two. The old build or image can't be found anymore, because it was deleted, its tag was moved, or there's a registry permission problem.

Three. Infrastructure or config changed. A secret, a feature flag, or an environment variable is now different and the old version can't start.

To help you properly, tell me:
- What you're deploying on, like Kubernetes, ECS, or plain VMs.

First, the app may just be starting slower than the health check allows. If the first check runs before the app has finished booting, warming caches or running migrations, it times out every time. Try raising the initial delay or the grace period and see if it passes.

Second, the app might be listening on the wrong port or address. A common one is binding to localhost, 127.0.0.1, when it needs to be 0.0.0.0. Then the app looks fine from inside the container but the health checker can't reach it. Also check that the port in your config matches the port the app actually uses.

Third, check the health endpoint itself. If it calls the database or another service, and that dependency is unreachable from the new environment, the endpoint hangs instead of failing quickly. Missing environment variables or secrets in the new release often cause this.

Fourth, look for a network rule or security group blocking the health checker's traffic. This is especially likely if something about the infrastructure changed recently.

The fastest way to narrow it down is to get a shell on the failing instance or container and request the health endpoint locally. If it responds there, the problem is networking or the port. If it hangs there too, the problem is in the app or one of its dependencies.

I can't see your deploy from here, so here's what I'd check first. When a health check times out the same way every time, it's usually one of these:

First, the port or address. The app might be listening on localhost instead of all interfaces, or on a different port than the health check uses. That's the most common cause.

Second, startup time. If the app needs longer to boot than the health check's grace period, for example while it runs migrations or warms a cache, it gets killed before it's ready. Try raising the initial delay or the timeout.

Third, the health endpoint itself. It might depend on a database or another service that the new environment can't reach. That shows up as a hang, not an error. Check the path too. One missing slash can do it.

Fourth, networking. A security group, firewall, or network policy might be blocking the health checker from reaching the container.

[pause] The fastest way to narrow it down is to look at the app's own logs from a failed attempt. Did it ever print that it was listening? And if you can, open a shell in the container and request the health endpoint locally.

[curious] What platform are you deploying to, and what do the app logs show right before the timeout? Send me those and we'll work out which one it is.

Sorry, that's a rough start to the day. The good news is that in Japan, lost wallets come back surprisingly often, so here's what I'd do, in order.

First, freeze your cards. Call each card issuer's lost card number, or freeze them in the app if your bank has one. Do this right away, even if you're hoping the wallet turns up. You can usually unfreeze a card later if it does.

Second, contact the railway. Things found on trains usually go to the station office or the line's lost and found center for a few days. Tell them which line you were on, roughly what time, which car if you remember, and what the wallet looks like. If it was a JR line, they have a lost and found inquiry service. Third, file a lost property report with the police. You can do it at any koban, or online for most prefectures. This matters because anything handed in eventually goes to the police. You'll also need the report number when you replace your ID.

Fourth, deal with your ID. If your My Number card was in there, call the My Number hotline to suspend it. That's zero one two zero, nine five, zero one seven eight. If your driver's license was in there, you can get it reissued at a license center, and they'll want the police report number. If you're not a Japanese national and your residence card was in the wallet, you need to apply for a new one at immigration within fourteen days, and bring the police report.

Also, if you had an IC card like Suica or Pasmo registered in your name, the station can block it and move your balance to a new card.
